o: Split the sentence into whitespace-separated words. A word is a price iff it is '$' followed by one or more digits and nothing else (so "$", "$1e5", "8$", "$10$" are not prices). Replace each price with '$' + (value * (100-discount) / 100) formatted to exactly two decimals. Prices have at most 10 digits, so they fit in 64-bit integers before scaling. Example 2 shows 100% discount yielding "$0.00".
k: Validate strictly: '$' + all digits + end of word; anything else passes through unchanged.
Compute discounted cents as an integer: value * (100 - discount), then format with two decimals.
Regex \$\d+(?![\w$]) captures prices precisely within a token-based or global substitution.

a.i: Split on spaces, test each word character-by-character (starts with '$', remainder all digits), transform qualifying words, and rejoin. No regex needed and easy to reason about.
s: For each word: price iff len>1, word[0]=='$', and every other char is a digit.
a.t: O(L) over the sentence length — each character examined a constant number of times.

a.i: Match \$\d+(?![\w$]) — a dollar sign, digits, and not followed by a letter, digit, or '$' — guaranteeing the match ends the token. Replace with the formatted discounted value in one pass.
s: Apply the regex globally over the sentence.
In the replacer, parse the matched digits, apply the discount, format to two decimals.

w: Watch the negative lookahead: without (?![\w$]), "$1e5" or "$10$" get corrupted. Floating rounding (e.g., x.xx5 cases) is avoided because value*(100-discount) is an exact integer number of cents; dividing by 100 then formatting is safe for these magnitudes.
